questions.subtopic: 1A1 Strategy, goals and objectives. Starting a risk program
questions.question: Asked to launch a risk program at an online travel agency, a risk practitioner receives a penetration test report with 120 findings from the CIO. What should the practitioner do FIRST?

options.A: Rank the 120 findings by their technical severity scores
options.B: Identify the business objectives the agency's key systems support
options.C: Choose controls for the findings that meet IT security objectives
options.D: Record each finding in the risk register as a separate risk

questions.key_concept: Risk management starts from business objectives; technical findings are causes that must be tied to objectives before they are rated.
questions.pre_read: Notice what the practitioner has been handed and what is still missing.
questions.correct_explanation: Risk is the effect of uncertainty on objectives, so a risk program starts by learning what the business is trying to achieve and which systems support it. Only then can the 120 findings become risk scenarios ranked by business impact. Recording each finding as a risk is the runner-up, but findings are causes; without objectives the register fills with technical issues no owner can prioritize.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because severity scores look objective. But technical severity is not business impact; a critical score on an unused system may matter less than a medium one on bookings.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the findings need controls and IT has its own objectives. But choosing controls before knowing the business objectives and risks they protect can waste money.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the register is the core risk record. But findings are causes, not risks; they need tying to objectives and impacts before they become register entries.

tips: Eliminate: A ranks by technical score rather than business impact, and C picks controls against IT objectives before the business risk is understood.
Final two: B beats D because risk is measured against objectives; findings become register risks only once they are tied to what the business needs.
Exam cue: when a program starts from a pile of technical findings, the FIRST step is to understand the business objectives.
questions.framework_ref: COBIT 2019 EDM03 (Ensured Risk Optimization); NIST CSF 2.0 GV.OC-01 (the organizational mission is understood and informs cybersecurity risk management)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1A1.1 Risk in Service of Business Objectives (exam trap: building the program from a vulnerability scan). Original online travel agency scenario written for KaiSip; no ISACA Review Manual, QAE or prep-bank text used. CRISC D1 pilot batch, 30 Oct 2026. Review fixes 30 Oct 2026 (blind test and standards audit): explanation reworded; distractors A and C lengthened, C now cites IT objectives so the lens word is not key-only; pre_read made neutral.

questions.subtopic: 1A1 Strategy, goals and objectives. Evaluating an IT goal
questions.question: A hospital's IT director proposes a target of 99.99 percent availability for every system. What should the risk practitioner consider MOST important when evaluating the proposal?

options.A: Which business goals require that level of availability
options.B: Whether monitoring tools can measure availability that precisely
options.C: The cost of reaching that availability for each system
options.D: Whether peer hospitals have adopted similar availability targets

questions.key_concept: In the COBIT 2019 goals cascade, IT goals are justified by the enterprise goals they support, not pursued for their own sake.
questions.pre_read: Notice that the target applies to every system alike, then ask what each option would tell you.
questions.correct_explanation: IT goals exist to serve enterprise goals, so the first test of a uniform 99.99 percent target is which clinical and business goals actually need it. Cost matters, and is the runner-up, but cost can only be weighed against the benefit to a business goal. Without that link there is nothing to compare it with, and many systems may need far less.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because a target must be measurable. But measurement is a later design question; it does not show whether the target is needed at all.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because near-perfect availability is expensive. But cost is weighed against business benefit, which is unknown until the target is linked to the goals it serves.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because benchmarks feel reassuring. But other hospitals' targets reflect their own goals and systems, not which of this hospital's services need near-continuous availability.

tips: Eliminate: D borrows other hospitals' targets instead of this hospital's needs, and B checks measurement before checking need.
Final two: A beats C because cost-benefit needs a benefit; the goals cascade justifies each IT goal by the business goal it supports.
Exam cue: when an IT goal is set for its own sake, trace it up to the enterprise goal before weighing cost or feasibility.
questions.framework_ref: COBIT 2019 APO02 (Managed Strategy); NIST CSF 2.0 GV.OC-01 (the organizational mission is understood and informs cybersecurity risk management)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1A1.2 The Goals Cascade and Strategic Change (exam trap: IT goals such as 99.99 percent uptime pursued for their own sake). Original hospital availability scenario written for KaiSip; no ISACA Review Manual, QAE or prep-bank text used. CRISC D1 pilot batch, 30 Oct 2026. Review fixes 30 Oct 2026 (blind test and standards audit): option wording tightened and lengths evened; pre_read made neutral; re-lettered (key D to A).

questions.subtopic: 1A2 Organizational structure, roles and responsibilities. Accepting residual risk
questions.question: After new controls are implemented, the residual risk of customer data exposure in a retailer's loyalty program is just inside appetite. Who should the risk practitioner confirm as the MOST appropriate person to accept it?

options.A: The marketing director who leads the loyalty program
options.B: The CISO who designed the new loyalty data controls
options.C: The risk analyst who assessed the residual risk
options.D: The platform manager who runs the loyalty application

questions.key_concept: Residual risk is accepted by the risk owner, the business manager accountable for the affected objective, not by control designers or analysts.
questions.pre_read: Note each role's link to the loyalty program: design, operation, analysis or leadership.
questions.correct_explanation: The risk owner is the business manager accountable for the objective the risk affects. The loyalty program's results belong to the marketing director, so they accept the residual risk. The CISO is the runner-up because they know the controls best, but designing controls makes them a control owner; accepting the business consequence of the remaining exposure is the program owner's decision.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the CISO is senior and understands the controls. But control design makes them a control owner, not the owner of the loyalty program's business risk.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the analyst knows the residual rating best. But the practitioner analyzes and recommends; accepting risk is a business decision for the owner.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because this manager runs the application daily. But operating the platform makes them a custodian or control owner, without authority over the program's objectives.

tips: Eliminate: C is the practitioner, who analyzes but never accepts, and D operates the platform as a custodian rather than owning the program's outcomes.
Final two: A beats B because risk is owned by the business manager accountable for the objective; designing controls makes the CISO a control owner.
Exam cue: for 'who accepts the risk', find the business manager whose objective or program bears the loss.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA Glossary (risk owner); NIST CSF 2.0 GV.RR-02 (roles, responsibilities and authorities related to cybersecurity risk management are established, communicated, understood and enforced)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1A2.2 Risk Owner, Control Owner and Risk Practitioner (compare table and isaca_rule). Original retail loyalty program scenario written for KaiSip; no ISACA Review Manual, QAE or prep-bank text used. CRISC D1 pilot batch, 30 Oct 2026. Review fixes 30 Oct 2026 (blind test and standards audit): key reworded (leads, not owns); CISO option lengthened; pre_read made neutral; stem says the controls are implemented (residual risk is measured after implementation).

questions.subtopic: 1A2 Organizational structure, roles and responsibilities. AI use case ownership
questions.question: A university's admissions office uses a vendor's AI model to rank applicants, and IT manages the vendor contract. Who should the risk practitioner propose as the MOST appropriate owner of the model's risk?

options.A: The IT manager who administers the vendor contract
options.B: The vendor that developed and maintains the model
options.C: The AI governance committee that reviews every AI use case
options.D: The admissions director whose decisions rely on the model

questions.key_concept: AI risk is owned by the business manager accountable for the use case; suppliers, administrators and committees play supporting roles.
questions.pre_read: Note each party's link to the model, who supplies, administers, oversees or uses it, and what each link gives authority over.
questions.correct_explanation: The risk owner is the business manager accountable for the outcome the model affects. Admissions decisions belong to the admissions director, so they own the risk, while IT, the vendor and the committee play supporting roles. The governance committee is the runner-up because it oversees AI, but a committee cannot be the one accountable person who decides on treatment and answers for admissions outcomes.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because IT manages the vendor relationship. But administering a contract gives no authority over admissions decisions or over the loss if the model ranks unfairly.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the vendor built and maintains the model. But outsourcing moves the work, not the accountability; the university still owns the risk to its admissions.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the committee oversees every AI use. But oversight is not ownership; one named business manager must be accountable for this use case's risk.

tips: Eliminate: A administers a contract without authority over admissions, and B is a supplier; outsourcing never transfers accountability for the university's risk.
Final two: D beats C because ownership needs one accountable business manager; a committee oversees AI risk but cannot own it.
Exam cue: for AI risk ownership, look past builders, hosts and committees to the manager whose decisions rely on the model.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA Glossary (risk owner); NIST AI 100-1 (AI RMF 1.0) GOVERN 2.1 (roles, responsibilities and lines of communication for AI risks are documented and clear)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1A2.3 RACI and Accountability, Including AI (exam traps: committee as accountable owner; builder as owner) and 1B5.3 (outsourcing moves the work, not the accountability). Original university admissions scenario written for KaiSip; no ISACA Review Manual, QAE or prep-bank text used. CRISC D1 pilot batch, 30 Oct 2026. Review fixes 30 Oct 2026 (blind test and standards audit): pre_read made neutral; framework_ref order changed (risk owner first); re-lettered (key C to D).

questions.subtopic: 1A2 Organizational structure, roles and responsibilities. Unowned risk at committee
questions.question: At a utility, the risk committee finds a high-rated supplier risk with no owner, and a member proposes the committee own it. What should the risk practitioner recommend as the BEST approach?

options.A: Record the committee as owner until a manager volunteers
options.B: Have procurement own it as the supplier contract holder
options.C: Ask senior management to assign a business manager as owner
options.D: Keep the risk under the risk function until settled

questions.key_concept: When a risk has no owner, senior management assigns an accountable business manager; committees oversee and the risk function monitors.
questions.pre_read: Notice what kind of body is offering to own the risk, and what that body's usual role is.
questions.correct_explanation: A risk needs one accountable owner with authority over the objective it threatens, and senior management assigns accountability when no one has it. A committee oversees and challenges; it cannot be that single owner, even for a while. Recording the committee as interim owner is the runner-up because it looks pragmatic, but it leaves a high-rated risk with no individual who decides and answers for the response.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting as a stopgap that keeps the risk visible. But a committee is not one accountable person, and waiting for a volunteer can last indefinitely.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because procurement holds the supplier contract. But managing a contract gives no authority over the business objective the supplier supports.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the risk function tracks the risk closely. But the second line monitors and challenges; owning a first-line risk would undermine its objectivity.

tips: Eliminate: B confuses contract management with ownership of the business objective, and D puts a first-line risk with the second line, which monitors rather than owns.
Final two: C beats A because accountability needs one named person; senior management assigns owners, while committees oversee.
Exam cue: when a risk has no owner, the BEST answer has senior management assign one, not a committee or the risk function.
questions.framework_ref: COBIT 2019 EDM01 (Ensured Governance Framework Setting and Maintenance); NIST CSF 2.0 GV.RR-02 (roles, responsibilities and authorities related to cybersecurity risk management are established, communicated, understood and enforced)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1A2.1 Board, Senior Management and the Risk Committee (exam trap: the committee is accountable for every risk it reviews) and 1A2.2 (exam trap: the practitioner owns risks nobody will take). Original utility supplier scenario written for KaiSip; no ISACA Review Manual, QAE or prep-bank text used. CRISC D1 pilot batch, 30 Oct 2026. Review fixes 30 Oct 2026 (blind test and standards audit): pre_read made neutral; re-lettered (key B to C).

questions.subtopic: 1A3 Organizational culture and ethics. Skipped verification steps
questions.question: A bank pays call center agents a bonus for calls closed per hour, and a risk analyst finds that recently trained agents often skip caller identity checks. What should the analyst recommend as MOST effective?

options.A: Retrain the agents on the caller identity verification procedure
options.B: Discipline agents who are found skipping identity checks
options.C: Add a weekly report of skipped checks to the dashboard
options.D: Change agent incentives to also reward completed identity checks

questions.key_concept: When incentives reward behavior that bypasses controls, rebalancing the incentive addresses the root cause; training and monitoring only support it.
questions.pre_read: Before choosing a fix, ask why people skip a step they have been trained to perform.
questions.correct_explanation: The bonus rewards speed alone, so agents skip checks to earn it: the incentive is the root cause. Changing it, for example by counting completed checks, removes the pressure that drives the behavior, and the call center's owner can make that change. Retraining is the runner-up, but these agents were recently trained; while pay rewards skipping it, training alone rarely changes what people do.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because training is the usual fix for skipped steps. But these agents were recently trained; the problem is motivation, and the bonus still rewards skipping.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it shows the rule is serious. But punishing individuals leaves the incentive in place and teaches staff to hide skipped checks.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because visibility helps oversight. But a report detects the problem after the fact; it does not remove the incentive that causes it.

tips: Eliminate: B punishes the symptom while the incentive stays, and C only detects skipped checks after they happen.
Final two: D beats A because the root cause is a pay scheme rewarding speed; training cannot outweigh an incentive that pays people to skip steps.
Exam cue: when people knowingly bypass a control to hit a target, look for the incentive and fix that first.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA Glossary (risk culture); NIST SP 800-39 Section 2.7 (Organizational Culture)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1A3.2 Incentives, Speaking Up and Escalation (isaca_rule: look for the incentive behind the behavior) and 1A3.1 (exam trap: training as the main lever). Original bank call center scenario written for KaiSip; no ISACA Review Manual, QAE or prep-bank text used. CRISC D1 pilot batch, 30 Oct 2026. Review fixes 30 Oct 2026 (blind test and standards audit): stem now says agents were recently trained; key reworded; pre_read and runner-up explanation updated.

questions.subtopic: 1A3 Organizational culture and ethics. Pressure to change a report
questions.question: Before a board meeting, a product director asks the risk analyst to remove an unfavorable penetration test result from the risk report, saying a fix is underway. What is the risk analyst's BEST response?

options.A: Remove the result and brief the board chair about it privately
options.B: Keep the result in the report and note the planned fix
options.C: Delay the report until the fix is complete and verified
options.D: Agree to the change requested by the product's risk owner

questions.key_concept: Practitioners disclose all significant facts objectively; context such as a planned fix is added, never used to omit or delay a finding.
questions.pre_read: Notice when the report will be used and who is asking for the change.
questions.correct_explanation: The ISACA Code of Professional Ethics asks members and certification holders to work with objectivity and to disclose all significant facts that, if left out, could distort the reported results. Keeping the finding and adding the planned fix gives the board an accurate, fair picture. Delaying the report is the runner-up because it sounds careful, but the board then meets without information it needs, which is the same distortion by another route.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the chair still hears about it. But the whole board relies on the report; a private briefing to one person leaves the record misleading.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the result may soon be out of date. But the board meets now, and holding back a significant fact distorts what it decides on.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the director is the risk owner. But owners decide responses, not which facts the board sees; altering the report breaches the duty to disclose.

tips: Eliminate: A informs one person while the record misleads the rest, and D confuses owning the response with controlling the facts.
Final two: B beats C because significant facts are disclosed when decisions are made; the planned fix is context, not a reason to wait.
Exam cue: under pressure to soften a report, keep the facts and add context; never omit or delay a significant finding.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA Code of Professional Ethics (inform appropriate parties of all significant facts); ISACA Code of Professional Ethics (objectivity, due diligence and professional care)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1A3.3 Professional Ethics and Ethical AI Use (isaca_rule: report what the analysis shows; exam trap: lowering the rating because the owner asks). Original product director scenario written for KaiSip; no ISACA Review Manual, QAE or prep-bank text used. CRISC D1 pilot batch, 30 Oct 2026. Review fixes 30 Oct 2026 (blind test and standards audit): self-justifying option D reworded; explanation reworded; pre_read made neutral; re-lettered (key A to B).

questions.subtopic: 1A4 Policies and standards. Stating management intent
questions.question: A risk practitioner at a hospital is helping update governance documents. Which document is the MOST appropriate place to state management's intent that patient data is protected according to its classification?

options.A: A standard setting minimum encryption for each class
options.B: A procedure for labeling patient records step by step
options.C: A policy that gives direction on protecting data
options.D: A guideline that suggests good handling practices

questions.key_concept: Policies state management's intent and are approved by senior management; standards, procedures and guidelines support them at lower levels.
questions.pre_read: Look at the kind of statement being made: broad intent, measurable rule, task steps or advice.
questions.correct_explanation: A policy states management's intent and direction, such as protecting patient data according to its classification, and senior management approves it so it carries enterprise authority. The standard is the runner-up because it is also mandatory, but it turns the policy into measurable specifics such as encryption strength; it supports the statement of intent rather than making it. Procedures and guidelines sit lower still.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because standards are mandatory too. But a standard sets specific, measurable requirements that support a policy; it does not state management's overall intent.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because labeling is how classification is applied. But a procedure gives task steps for staff, not management's direction.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because guidelines describe good practice. But guidelines are advisory, so management's intent placed there would not be binding.

tips: Eliminate: B gives task steps for staff and D is advisory, so neither can carry management's binding intent.
Final two: C beats A because intent and direction belong in a policy; a standard makes that intent measurable underneath it.
Exam cue: 'management's intent' or 'direction' points to a policy approved by senior management.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA Glossary (policy); NIST CSF 2.0 GV.PO-01 (policy for managing cybersecurity risks is established based on organizational context, cybersecurity strategy and priorities and is communicated and enforced)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1A4.1 The Policy Hierarchy (compare table: policy, standard, procedure, guideline). Original hospital governance scenario written for KaiSip; no ISACA Review Manual, QAE or prep-bank text used. CRISC D1 pilot batch, 30 Oct 2026. Review fixes 30 Oct 2026 (blind test and standards audit): options rebalanced to parallel length; key no longer the only option echoing the stem.

questions.subtopic: 1A4 Policies and standards. New AI tool in use
questions.question: A risk practitioner at an engineering consultancy without an AI policy learns some designers upload client drawings to a public generative AI service, but not how often. What should the practitioner do FIRST?

options.A: Block the AI service at the network perimeter immediately
options.B: Assess whether designers know their confidentiality duties
options.C: Draft an AI acceptable use policy for senior management approval
options.D: Assess the exposure of client data through the AI service

questions.key_concept: When staff adopt an AI tool before any policy exists, the practitioner first assesses the exposure; policy and controls follow from it.
questions.pre_read: Notice what the practitioner knows and does not yet know about the uploads.
questions.correct_explanation: On CRISC items, a new risk is analyzed before a response is chosen. Assessing how much client data reaches the service, and what that could cost the firm, tells the owner how urgent the issue is and what a policy must cover. Drafting the policy is the runner-up and will likely follow, but writing rules before understanding the exposure risks a policy that misses the real problem.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because it stops uploads at once. But blocking is a response the business chooses after the risk is understood, and it may push use onto personal devices.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because confidentiality duties apply. But checking what designers know neither measures the data exposure nor gives staff rules for AI tools.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the policy gap is real. But the policy should follow from the assessed exposure, so it addresses what designers actually upload and why.

tips: Eliminate: A imposes a response before the risk is analyzed, and B checks staff knowledge, which neither measures the exposure nor sets rules.
Final two: D beats C because analysis comes before response; the assessed exposure tells management what the AI use policy must address.
Exam cue: when new technology outpaces policy, assess the risk FIRST; the policy update follows from what the assessment finds.
questions.framework_ref: COBIT 2019 APO12 (Managed Risk); NIST CSF 2.0 GV.PO-02 (policy for managing cybersecurity risks is reviewed, updated, communicated and enforced to reflect changes)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1A4.3 Policy Review and AI Acceptable Use (isaca_rule: when new technology outpaces policy, analyze the risk and recommend an update; exam trap: block every AI tool). Original engineering consultancy scenario written for KaiSip; no ISACA Review Manual, QAE or prep-bank text used. CRISC D1 pilot batch, 30 Oct 2026. Review fixes 30 Oct 2026 (blind test and standards audit): stem now says the extent of uploads is unknown; a distractor now uses assess; pre_read made neutral; re-lettered (key B to D).

questions.subtopic: 1A5 Business processes and resilience. Continuity plan testing
questions.question: A risk practitioner at a manufacturer finds the payroll continuity plan was last tested two years ago, as a document walkthrough. What is the BEST recommendation?

options.A: Run a realistic payroll disruption exercise with the process owner
options.B: Update the plan to reflect current payroll staff and suppliers
options.C: Have the payroll process owner re-approve the plan each year
options.D: Have IT test failover of the payroll application to the backup site

questions.key_concept: Continuity plans are verified by realistic exercises with the process owner; paper reviews and IT failover alone do not prove the business can continue.
questions.pre_read: Notice how the plan was tested and how long ago. Ask what a walkthrough can and cannot show.
questions.correct_explanation: A walkthrough checks the document, not whether payroll can actually run during a disruption, and two years is a long gap. A realistic exercise with the payroll process owner tests people, workarounds and dependencies, and its gaps go to the risk register. Updating the plan is the runner-up and worth doing, but an updated plan that is still untested remains an unverified control.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because plans go stale. But updating the contents does not prove the plan works; it still needs a realistic test.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because owner approval shows commitment. But re-approving the document is not a test; it shows the plan was read, not that payroll can run during a disruption.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because system recovery matters to payroll. But failover tests the DRP for one application; it does not show the payroll process can continue.

tips: Eliminate: D tests system failover rather than the business process, and C treats re-approving a document as proof the plan works.
Final two: A beats B because only a realistic test shows the plan works; an updated but untested plan is still unverified.
Exam cue: for continuity plans, prefer realistic tests owned by the business over paper reviews or IT-only failovers.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1 Section 3.5 (Plan Testing, Training, and Exercises); COBIT 2019 DSS04 (Managed Continuity)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1A5.2 Continuity and Recovery Plans as Risk Responses (exam traps: a DRP test proves resilience; a walkthrough is enough testing). Original manufacturer payroll scenario written for KaiSip; no ISACA Review Manual, QAE or prep-bank text used. CRISC D1 pilot batch, 30 Oct 2026. Review fixes 30 Oct 2026 (blind test and standards audit): sign-off distractor now has the process owner re-approve the plan; key reworded; re-lettered (key D to A).

questions.subtopic: 1A6 Organizational asset management. AI model inventory record
questions.question: An insurer's risk practitioner is inventorying the AI models used in claims, pricing and marketing. Which attribute is MOST important to record for each model so its risk can be managed?

options.A: The named business owner who answers for the model's use
options.B: The model version and the sources of its training data
options.C: The cloud platform owner and hardware the model runs on
options.D: The number of staff who query the model each month

questions.key_concept: Every inventoried asset, including an AI model, needs an accountable business owner; classification and risk decisions depend on that owner.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the inventory is for, then test each attribute against that purpose.
questions.correct_explanation: An inventory supports risk management only if each entry leads to someone who can decide. The accountable business owner classifies the model, accepts its risk and answers for how it is used, so ownership comes first. Version and training data sources are the runner-up and should be recorded too, but without an owner nobody acts on what those details reveal about the model's risk.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because version and data lineage drive AI risk. But these details inform an assessment; without an owner, no one is accountable for acting on them.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because hosting affects security. But the platform owner is a custodian; it does not say who decides how much risk the model may carry.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because heavy use suggests importance. But usage volume is not business impact, and it names no one to classify the model or accept its risk.

tips: Eliminate: C records a custodial hosting detail and D records usage volume; neither identifies who decides on the model's risk.
Final two: A beats B because ownership comes first; classification, assessment and risk acceptance all need an accountable owner to act.
Exam cue: for any asset inventory question, including AI models, a named business owner is the attribute everything else depends on.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 (AI RMF 1.0) GOVERN 1.6 (mechanisms are in place to inventory AI systems); COBIT 2019 BAI09 (Managed Assets)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1A6.3 Cloud, SaaS and AI Assets in the Inventory and 1A6.1 Asset Inventory and Ownership (isaca_rule: ownership comes first). Original insurer AI inventory scenario written for KaiSip; no ISACA Review Manual, QAE or prep-bank text used. CRISC D1 pilot batch, 30 Oct 2026. Review fixes 30 Oct 2026 (blind test and standards audit): stem states the inventory's purpose; key reworded; platform-owner distractor added; pre_read made neutral.

questions.subtopic: 1B1 Enterprise risk management (ERM). Ratings that do not match
questions.question: A hospital network's IT risk register rates three scenarios, including ransomware, as critical, yet its enterprise register shows no technology risk above moderate. What should the risk practitioner conclude is the MOST likely cause?

options.A: The enterprise risk committee has accepted the ransomware risk
options.B: IT ratings are not normalized to the enterprise rating scale
options.C: IT has overstated the likelihood of a ransomware attack
options.D: Cyber insurance has transferred the ransomware risk to the insurer

questions.key_concept: IT risk must be normalized to enterprise scales and rolled into the enterprise register; otherwise serious IT risks vanish from the enterprise view.
questions.pre_read: Count how many risks the mismatch affects before deciding whether one rating or the process behind the registers is at fault.
questions.correct_explanation: When three critical IT risks all appear no higher than moderate at enterprise level, the likeliest cause is integration: IT ratings are not normalized to the enterprise scale when they are rolled into the enterprise register. That is a systemic gap. IT overstating ransomware likelihood is the runner-up, but it would explain only that one scenario, not why every critical IT risk drops out of the enterprise view.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because accepted risks receive less attention. But acceptance does not change a risk's rating; an accepted critical risk stays critical in the register.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because IT teams sometimes rate technical threats high. But one overstated scenario cannot explain why three critical IT risks all appear no higher than moderate.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because insurance is a common ransomware response. But insurance shares part of the financial loss; disruption to patient care and reputation stays with the hospital.

tips: Eliminate: A assumes acceptance lowers a rating, and D assumes insurance moves the whole risk; insurance shares only part of the financial loss.
Final two: B beats C because the mismatch covers all three critical risks; one overstated rating cannot explain a pattern across the registers.
Exam cue: when IT and enterprise views of risk disagree, suspect missing integration and inconsistent scales before blaming one rating.
questions.framework_ref: NIST IR 8286 Rev. 1 Section 3.8 (Creating and Maintaining an Enterprise-Level Cybersecurity Risk Register); NIST CSF 2.0 GV.RM-06 (a standardized method for calculating, documenting, categorizing and prioritizing cybersecurity risks is established and communicated)

questions.subtopic: 1B1 Enterprise risk management (ERM). Approving the framework
questions.question: A risk practitioner has drafted an updated IT risk management framework for a logistics company. Whose approval is MOST important to give it authority over every business unit?

options.A: The risk practitioner who drafted the framework
options.B: The IT steering committee that oversees technology projects
options.C: The internal audit function that will later review it
options.D: Senior management, through the executive committee

questions.key_concept: Senior management approves the risk management framework, giving it authority across the enterprise; the practitioner drafts and maintains it.
questions.pre_read: Notice the scope the framework must cover, then check each option's authority against it.
questions.correct_explanation: A risk management framework binds every unit, so it needs approval from senior management, here through the executive committee, which can require adoption across the business; the board then oversees that it works. The IT steering committee is the runner-up because the framework covers IT risk, but the committee governs technology projects and cannot bind business units outside its remit.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the author knows the framework best. But drafting is the practitioner's role; approval must come from leaders with authority over the whole enterprise.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the framework concerns IT risk. But the steering committee governs technology projects; it lacks authority to bind the business units that own the risks.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because audit gives an independent view. But approving the framework would impair audit's independence when it later assesses whether the framework works.

tips: Eliminate: A confuses authorship with authority, and C would impair audit's independence when it later reviews the framework.
Final two: D beats B because the framework must bind every business unit; only senior management has that enterprise-wide authority.
Exam cue: frameworks, policies and appetite are approved by senior management or the board; specialists draft and advise.

questions.subtopic: 1B2 Lines of defense. Offer to design controls
questions.question: Internal audit offers to design the access controls for a bank's new payroll system so they pass next year's audit. What should the risk practitioner advise as the BEST approach?

options.A: Accept audit's offer to design the payroll access controls
options.B: Have the second-line risk team design them as control owner
options.C: Have the payroll system owner design them, with audit advising
options.D: Let audit design them if a different audit team reviews them

questions.key_concept: The first line designs and runs controls; internal audit may advise but must not design controls it will later assure.
questions.pre_read: Place each party in its line of defense. Ask which line should build the controls and which must stay independent.
questions.correct_explanation: The first line owns its risks and designs and runs the controls; internal audit, the third line, may advise but must stay independent of what it will later assure. Having the payroll system owner design the controls with audit's input keeps both roles intact. A second-line design is the runner-up, but it takes control ownership from the first line and leaves the risk team challenging its own work.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because audit knows what passes review. But designing controls puts audit in a management role and impairs its independence when it audits them.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the risk team is expert and close to the business. But the second line oversees and challenges; designing and owning controls belongs to the first line.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because rotating reviewers sounds like a safeguard. But it is still the audit function assuring its own design, so its independence is impaired.

tips: Eliminate: A and D both have audit design controls it will later assure; a different reviewing team does not change that the audit function built them.
Final two: C beats B because the first line designs, owns and runs its controls; the second-line risk team advises and challenges but does not own them.
Exam cue: in lines-of-defense items, the first line designs and runs controls; audit advises but never builds what it will assure.

questions.subtopic: 1B2 Lines of defense. Second-line independence
questions.question: A new chief risk officer proposes that the second-line risk team stop advising business units on control design, to be as independent as internal audit. What is the risk practitioner's BEST advice?

options.A: Keep advising on design while challenging owners' risk ratings
options.B: Stop advising and review owners' controls after they are built
options.C: Refer business units to internal audit for design advice instead
options.D: Move the risk team's reporting line to the audit committee

questions.key_concept: The second line advises and challenges from within management and needs objectivity; full independence is the third line's requirement.
questions.pre_read: Ask which line the risk team belongs to and what that line needs in order to do its job well.
questions.correct_explanation: The second line sits within management on purpose: it advises the first line and challenges its ratings and controls. It needs independence from the first-line work it challenges, plus a route to escalate, but not internal audit's independence from management. Moving its reporting line to the audit committee is the runner-up because it looks stronger, but it would cast the second line as a second audit function and weaken its role inside management.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because reviewing after the fact feels more independent. But advising on design is a core second-line job; late review denies owners risk input when changes are cheapest.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because audit may give advice. But making audit the business's routine source of design advice moves second-line work to the third line and strains its independence.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it looks like stronger independence. But the second line belongs to management; it needs access to the board, not an audit-style reporting line.

tips: Eliminate: B drops a core second-line job, and C moves routine design advice to internal audit, which must stay independent of what it later assures.
Final two: A beats D because the second line needs objectivity within management; audit-level independence and reporting belong to the third line.
Exam cue: independence from management is the third line's requirement; the second line needs objectivity, challenge and escalation rights while staying inside management.

questions.subtopic: 1B3 Risk profile. Profile after an acquisition
questions.question: A software company completes the acquisition of a smaller competitor with its own IT systems, and the enterprise risk profile was refreshed two months ago. What should the risk practitioner do FIRST?

options.A: Wait for the next scheduled annual update of the risk profile
options.B: Identify and assess the acquired company's risks for the profile
options.C: Assess how existing controls could extend to the acquired systems
options.D: Ask the acquired company to maintain its own separate risk profile

questions.key_concept: Major business changes such as acquisitions trigger an immediate update of the risk profile, starting with identifying and assessing new risks.
questions.pre_read: Notice what changed since the profile was last refreshed and what each option does first.
questions.correct_explanation: An acquisition is a trigger event: it changes the business, the assets and the threats, so the profile no longer reflects reality even though it is only two months old. Identifying and assessing the acquired company's risks, then aggregating them into the profile, comes first. Extending existing controls is the runner-up, but choosing controls before the new risks are analyzed may miss what the acquired systems need.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the profile is recent. But the acquisition changes the risk landscape now; waiting a year leaves leaders deciding on an outdated picture.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because consistent controls are likely. But reviewing controls before identifying the new risks gets the order wrong; the acquired systems may face risks those controls never addressed.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the acquired company knows its own systems. But a separate profile keeps its risks out of the enterprise view that leaders use to decide.

tips: Eliminate: A treats the profile as a fixed annual document, and D keeps the acquired risks outside the enterprise view.
Final two: B beats C because risks are analyzed before controls are chosen; the acquired systems may need controls the company does not have.
Exam cue: a merger, acquisition, new market or major incident is a trigger to update the risk profile now, starting with assessment.

questions.subtopic: 1B4 Risk appetite and risk tolerance. Expressing a tolerance
questions.question: A bank's board states a low appetite for disruption to customer services. Which statement should the risk practitioner propose as the BEST risk tolerance supporting this appetite?

options.A: The bank will avoid disruption to customer-facing services
options.B: The bank could survive a five-day outage without failing
options.C: Online banking may be unavailable no more than two hours a month
options.D: Customer service outages will be reported to the board quarterly

questions.key_concept: Risk tolerance turns broad appetite into measurable limits for specific objectives or metrics, inside the enterprise's risk capacity.
questions.pre_read: Sort the four statements into appetite, tolerance, capacity or something else before choosing.
questions.correct_explanation: Risk tolerance is the acceptable variation around appetite, usually a measurable limit for a specific objective or metric. Two hours of online banking downtime a month turns a low appetite for disruption into a limit that can be monitored and breached. The avoidance statement is the runner-up because it supports the appetite, but it is broad and unmeasurable, so it restates appetite rather than setting a tolerance.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because it matches the board's intent. But it is a broad statement with no measurable limit, so it restates appetite instead of setting a tolerance.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it is measurable. But the most loss the bank could survive describes risk capacity, the outer boundary, not the limit it wants to operate within.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because reporting supports oversight. But a reporting schedule sets no limit on how much disruption is acceptable.

tips: Eliminate: B describes risk capacity, the survival limit, and D sets a reporting schedule rather than a limit.
Final two: C beats A because a tolerance is a measurable limit for a specific metric; the avoidance statement is broad and only restates appetite.
Exam cue: appetite is broad and set by the board; tolerance is a measurable limit; capacity is what the enterprise can survive.

questions.subtopic: 1B4 Risk appetite and risk tolerance. Indicator above tolerance
questions.question: A logistics firm's confirmed KRI for failed nightly backups has exceeded tolerance for two weeks while IT handles it as a routine ticket. What is the risk practitioner's BEST action?

options.A: Raise the KRI threshold to match current backup performance
options.B: Hold the breach for the risk owner's next quarterly review
options.C: Ask IT to resolve the ticket quickly and report back once closed
options.D: Escalate the breach to the risk owner with an impact estimate

questions.key_concept: A confirmed tolerance breach is escalated promptly to the risk owner with its impact; it is a governance decision, not a technical ticket.
questions.pre_read: Notice how long the indicator has been over its limit and who currently knows about it.
questions.correct_explanation: A tolerance breach means the firm is carrying more risk than its leaders agreed to, so it is a governance event, not just a ticket. With the data confirmed, the practitioner escalates to the risk owner with the likely business impact, so the owner can decide on interim measures or formal acceptance. Letting IT close the ticket is the runner-up, but the owner stays unaware while backups keep failing.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the threshold no longer matches reality. But only the level that set a tolerance can change it, and moving the line to fit results hides risk.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it does involve the owner. But two weeks of failed backups above tolerance needs a decision now, not at a routine quarterly review.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because IT is already working the issue. But a fix in progress does not inform the risk owner, who must decide while risk exceeds tolerance.

tips: Eliminate: A moves the threshold to fit the result, and B holds a live breach for routine reporting instead of escalating it promptly.
Final two: D beats C because a tolerance breach needs the risk owner's decision; IT fixing the ticket leaves the owner unaware of risk above limits.
Exam cue: a confirmed KRI breach goes to the risk owner, with its impact, promptly; it is not left in a technical ticket queue.

questions.subtopic: 1B4 Risk appetite and risk tolerance. Request to set appetite
questions.question: Before a strategy offsite, a hospital's board asks the risk practitioner to set the organization's appetite for cybersecurity risk. What is the practitioner's BEST approach?

options.A: Adopt the appetite statement of a similar peer hospital
options.B: Set the appetite at the current risk profile's level
options.C: Prepare analysis and options for the board to set appetite
options.D: Ask the CISO to decide the cybersecurity risk appetite

questions.key_concept: The board and senior management set risk appetite; the practitioner supplies analysis, capacity data and options to support their decision.
questions.pre_read: Notice who is being asked to decide, and check whether that role has the authority to make the decision.
questions.correct_explanation: Risk appetite reflects the enterprise's strategy, capacity and stakeholder expectations, which the board and senior management own, so the practitioner informs and facilitates rather than deciding. Preparing loss data, capacity estimates and options lets the board set appetite itself. Asking the CISO is the runner-up because cybersecurity is their field, but it hands the decision to another specialist instead of returning it to the governing body.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because benchmarks save time. But a peer's appetite reflects its own strategy and capacity, not this hospital's.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it is grounded in data. But the current profile shows where risk is today; appetite states where leaders want it to be.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the CISO knows cybersecurity best. But expertise does not confer authority; appetite is a board and senior management decision.

tips: Eliminate: A copies a peer whose strategy and capacity differ, and B mistakes the current profile for the desired appetite.
Final two: C beats D because appetite belongs to the board and senior management; handing it to the CISO still leaves a specialist deciding.
Exam cue: when asked to 'set' appetite, the practitioner supplies analysis and options; leaders make the decision.

questions.subtopic: 1B5 Risk frameworks, legal, regulatory and contractual requirements. Clean examination result
questions.question: A fintech passes its regulatory examination with no findings, and the CFO proposes cutting the IT risk budget because compliance shows risk is low. What should the risk practitioner advise as MOST appropriate?

options.A: Support the budget cut in line with the examination result
options.B: Explain that compliance is a minimum and other risks need assessment
options.C: Keep the full budget until a second examination confirms the result
options.D: Move the IT risk budget to assessing upcoming compliance rules

questions.key_concept: Compliance shows minimum obligations are met, not that overall IT risk is low; risks outside regulation still need assessment against appetite.
questions.pre_read: Notice what the examination actually tested, and what the CFO concludes from it.
questions.correct_explanation: Regulations set minimum duties for specific harms, so a clean examination shows those duties were met, not that IT risk overall is low. Risks such as outages, new threats or supplier failures may fall outside any rule, so budgets should follow assessed risk against appetite. Waiting for a second examination is the runner-up because it sounds prudent, but another clean result would prove the same narrow point.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the examiners found nothing. But an examination tests compliance with specific rules; it does not assess every risk to the fintech's objectives.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it delays a risky cut. But a second clean examination would still show only compliance, not the level of the fintech's wider IT risk.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it seems to protect compliance. But it moves money from managing risk to compliance alone, while risks outside regulation stay unassessed.

tips: Eliminate: A treats a clean examination as proof of low risk, and D narrows spending to compliance while risks outside regulation go unassessed.
Final two: B beats C because compliance is a floor; a second clean examination would still say nothing about risks no rule covers.
Exam cue: compliant does not mean low risk; budgets and responses follow assessed risk against appetite, not examination results alone.
